parts.note: take-off reads as an aircraft leaving the ground, but it means taking off one's clothes, after which one dashes naked past onlookers

explanation.surface: An aircraft climbs from the runway and then roars over the crowd in a flypast.
explanation.walkthrough: The aviation picture misleads: 'take-off' is undressing and 'fly past' is running quickly by, as a naked prankster does at a sports match.
explanation.definitionFit: To run naked through a public place, typically for a dare, is a well-known slang sense.

definitions.meaning: walks with an awkward, dragging, unsteady gait
a state of total disorder or chaos

explanation.surface: Someone staggers unsteadily into the officers' dining room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The mess' suggests a military dining hall, but it simply means chaos; 'into the' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: To shamble is to walk with a shuffling gait, and a complete muddle or chaotic scene is also called by this noun.

clue.text: Hope for the lost and sick

definitions.text: Hope for the lost and sick

parts.words: Hope for the lost and sick
parts.note: what people wish for when property has gone missing, and also what invalids wish for: getting it back, and getting well

explanation.surface: A charity appeal offers hope to lost souls and the ill.
explanation.walkthrough: The one word covers both halves: lost goods are got back, and the sick get better.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun covers both retrieving missing property and returning to health after illness.

clue.text: Indian currency goes up and down

indicators.note: in a down clue the word reads the same whether read upwards or downwards, so the letters form a palindrome

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: The Indian rupee fluctuates in value on the markets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes up and down' looks like a market report, but in a down clue it says the word reads the same up the grid as down it.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a former coin of India, worth one sixteenth of a rupee.

clue.text: He kills a couple of fools in the end

indicators.note: places the little word in at the finish of the assembled letters
a couple means two, so the word for fools is written twice in a row

parts.note: an ass is a foolish person
taken as written

explanation.surface: A murderer finishes off a pair of idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: The fools look like the killer's victims, but they spell out his title: 'a couple of' says write that word twice, and 'the end' says where the small word goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A hired murderer is someone who kills, especially a public figure, for political or paid motives.

clue.text: Dead and buried a fathom deep

definitions.meaning: deceased and in the grave
a fathom is a nautical measure of six feet, so this is that distance below the surface

explanation.surface: A drowned sailor lies at the bottom, a fathom down.
explanation.walkthrough: A fathom equals six feet, the traditional depth of a grave, so both halves describe the same phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for being in the grave, and literally gives a depth of one nautical fathom.

definitions.meaning: playing cards or dice faces marked with a single pip
people outstandingly skilled at something

explanation.surface: One person picks out the specialists in a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One spots' reads as 'somebody notices', but it means cards bearing a single spot; experts are also called by the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The card marked with one pip shares its name with top performers or masters of a skill.

clue.text: I left aspirin, ordered for injury

indicators.note: put in a new order, so the remaining letters are rearranged
the letter I departs from the word aspirin, so it is removed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone forgot their painkillers and has to cope with a pulled muscle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' takes I out of ASPIRIN to leave ASPRIN, and 'ordered' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrenched ankle or wrist with torn ligaments is a common physical hurt of this kind.

definitions.meaning: antagonism or bad feeling between rivals
the stylus lowered onto a vinyl disc to play it

explanation.surface: Enmity is formally logged in the minutes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on record' sounds like making something official, but it describes the stylus resting on a gramophone disc.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporting rivalry with bad blood is called this, and so is the pointed stylus of a record player.

indicators.note: wild suggests disorder, so the letters of dances are scrambled

explanation.surface: People rise from their seats to join some frenzied dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: To rise or climb upward is a synonym of getting up.

parts.note: a play on hubbub: the bar running from one wheel hub across to the other wheel hub

explanation.surface: A noisy hubbub, written with a hyphen.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue looks like a misspelt hubbub; read it as hub to hub, the fixed bar linking two wheels on a cart.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the bar or beam on which a pair of opposite wheels turn, joining one hub to the other.

clue.text: Pleasing to see in a church but not in a pub!

definitions.text: Pleasing to see in a church but not in a pub!

parts.words: Pleasing to see in a church but not in a pub!
parts.note: coloured windows are admired in churches, but a dirty, marked drinking vessel is unwelcome in a bar

explanation.surface: Something welcome in a place of worship is unwelcome in a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: In a church the phrase means coloured windows; in a pub it would describe a grubby, marked tumbler.
explanation.definitionFit: Coloured glass in church windows is admired, while a marked tumbler at the bar is not.

indicators.note: signals that the word is spoken, so its sound rather than its spelling counts

parts.note: bevvy is British slang for an alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: A group meets up for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: BEVVY is informal British for an alcoholic drink; said out loud it matches the collective noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A group or flock, such as of quails or of young women, is a collective term synonymous with a gathering.

clue.text: The navy is often so perplexed

definitions.meaning: warships spend much time away on the ocean
confused and bewildered

explanation.surface: Sailors in the fleet are frequently confused.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally means out on the ocean and idiomatically means bewildered or lost.

parts.note: reads as someone who withdraws cash, but a drawer is also the sliding box in a shop counter where takings are kept

explanation.surface: Someone withdraws cash from the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawer' looks like a person who draws money out; it is the cash compartment of a shop counter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cash register or its money compartment in a shop is called by this word.

definitions.meaning: to scatter fine droplets over
a small bunch or sprig of blooms

explanation.surface: A gardener waters a few blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: To mist something with liquid is one sense; a single branch bearing blossoms is another.

indicators.note: about suggests turning things around, so the letters of hangs are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone loafs around complaining that life is a dull chore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grind' looks like a tedious task, but here it is a verb: to grind the teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: To grit or grind the teeth together, in anger or pain, is the verb meant.

clue.text: Painfully noisy in the grain division

definitions.meaning: loud enough to hurt one's hearing
cutting apart the heads of cereal crops, such as corn or wheat

explanation.surface: Threshing in a granary makes a painful racket.
explanation.walkthrough: An ear is the seed head of a cereal, so dividing it gives the second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Deafeningly loud is the idiom, and literally it is the cleaving of the seed heads of corn.

parts.note: openers are the things that unlock doors, and the openings are the slots in locks they fit into

explanation.surface: Gaps in a cricket field for the opening batsmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Openers' looks like the first batters in cricket, but it means the things that open locks.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the slots in a lock into which a key is inserted to turn it.

clue.text: They will keep on watch in the ship

indicators.note: the word for watch is set inside the letters for the ship

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, a prefix in ship names
ticker is informal for a watch or clock

explanation.surface: Sailors stand guard during their watch aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' looks like a turn of guard duty, but it is a timepiece, slangily TICKER.
explanation.definitionFit: Adhesive labels cling, so they remain in place; persistent people who never give up are also called this.

clue.text: Introduce objectives to for the hunt to live within its income

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Introduce objectives to for the hunt to live within its income': 'to for' is garbled; MAKE + ENDS + MEET needs a word for MAKE that the held text does not give, and an exact-text search found no source
annotationWithheld.clue: Introduce objectives to for the hunt to live within its income

clue.text: May describe a bridge card he shuffled

indicators.note: cards are shuffled into a new order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: In a card game a player shuffles the deck for bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' and 'card' suggest the card game, but the bridge is a span with a curved shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge supported on a curved span is described as having a bowed, vaulted shape.

definitions.meaning: a picture made from small fitted pieces of tile or glass
relating to Moses, who brought down the commandments

explanation.surface: A labourer paid by the piece follows the rules of a legislator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece-work' looks like pay per item; it is art made of pieces. The capitalised sense means relating to Moses.
explanation.definitionFit: Tessellated artwork made of tiles is one sense; the adjective relating to Moses, giver of the Ten Commandments, is the other.

indicators.note: signals that the word is spoken, so its sound counts

parts.note: rude in its old sense means rough, unrefined or untilled

explanation.surface: A patch of land is reported to be lying wild.
explanation.walkthrough: A ROOD is an old British measure of land, a quarter of an acre; 'uncultivated' looks like it describes the area but supplies RUDE.
explanation.definitionFit: An old English unit of land measurement equal to a quarter of an acre.

clue.text: She takes a long time to grasp the point

indicators.note: to grasp means to hold within, so the point goes inside

parts.note: ages means a very long period
N is north, one of the compass points

explanation.surface: A woman needs ages before she understands the gist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The point' looks like the gist of an argument, but it is a compass point, N for north.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name stands for the pronoun, as a crossword convention.

clue.text: In which I combine style and elegance

indicators.note: in means the letters are found inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A fashion writer explains how she blends flair with grace.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'whi-CH I C-ombine'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stylish elegance is the noun sense of this French-derived word for fashionable smartness.

definitions.meaning: something put on the foot and worn
the curved block that presses against a wheel

explanation.surface: A component of a braking system has worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worn' reads as worn out, but it means an item of footwear one wears.
explanation.definitionFit: Footwear is something worn, and the friction block in a drum brake bears the same name.

clue.text: Cricket ground lacking parking is cause of irritation

indicators.note: lacking means without, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: the pitch is the strip in a cricket ground where the ball is bowled
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A cricket ground with nowhere to park annoys the fans.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the pitch is the central strip of the field; 'lacking' removes P to leave the itch.
explanation.definitionFit: An urge to scratch the skin is a source of annoyance, physical or figurative.

definitions.note: the answer is a cry of approval itself, not a verb

indicators.note: the word is given more than once, so it is written twice

parts.note: to hear a case in court is to try it

explanation.surface: Someone keeps attempting to show they agree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' looks like attempt; it is the legal sense, as a judge hears or tries a case.
explanation.definitionFit: The cry, heard in Parliament, is a call of agreement used to applaud a speaker.

parts.note: TT stands for teetotal, a non-drinker
Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general in the American Civil War

explanation.surface: A former British premier is described as an abstinent military officer.
explanation.walkthrough: Clement ATTLEE was Labour prime minister 1945-51; 'general' looks like an adjective but names Lee.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement Attlee led Britain's postwar Labour government from 1945 to 1951.

definitions.meaning: to shrink or diminish
to press out the creases from clothes

explanation.surface: Use the iron less often.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a pun: to de-crease clothing is to remove its folds.
explanation.definitionFit: To diminish or decline is one sense; read as de-crease it means smoothing fabric with a hot iron.

indicators.note: read as re-places, putting the letters in new positions

explanation.surface: An archbishop takes over from the church ushers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' suggests an archbishop to match ushers, but it is the monkey; 're-places' rearranges USHERS.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhesus macaque is a South Asian monkey, a member of the primate order.
